summary: Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist used as the antidote for known or suspected opioid overdose, rapidly reversing respiratory and CNS depression. It is given IV (fastest), IM, SC, or intranasally (Narcan). Because its duration of action is shorter than that of many opioids, re-sedation (re-narcotization) can occur, so repeat dosing and continued monitoring are essential. It may precipitate acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.

moa: Naloxone is a pure competitive antagonist at opioid (predominantly mu) receptors; it displaces opioid agonists from the receptor and blocks their effects, reversing respiratory depression and sedation. It has essentially no pharmacologic activity in the absence of opioids.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to naloxone or any excipient
relative: Patients maintained on partial/mixed agonists such as buprenorphine (reversal may be incomplete)

preg: Crosses the placenta; may precipitate withdrawal in an opioid-dependent mother and fetus. Use in pregnancy when needed to treat life-threatening opioid overdose.
lact: It is not known whether naloxone is excreted in human milk; use with caution. A single emergency dose is unlikely to harm a breastfed infant.
renal: Safety and efficacy in renal insufficiency or failure have not been established; use with caution.
hepatic: Safety and efficacy in liver disease have not been established; use with caution (extensive hepatic metabolism).

major: Buprenorphine - slow receptor dissociation may require larger/repeated naloxone doses for reversal
Partial/mixed opioid agonist-antagonists (pentazocine) - reversal may be incomplete
moderate: Opioid agonists - naloxone reverses their effects and precipitates withdrawal in dependence
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; does not reverse alcohol or non-opioid sedative effects

common: Precipitated opioid withdrawal (body aches, sweating, tachycardia, runny nose, sneezing, yawning, piloerection, nausea/vomiting, abdominal cramps)

missed: Not a scheduled medication - naloxone is given as needed for acute opioid overdose. Repeat every 2-3 minutes if the person does not respond or if opioid effects recur.
overdose: Naloxone itself has very low toxicity. Excess doses in opioid-dependent patients precipitate acute withdrawal, which is managed supportively (fluids, antiemetics, symptom control). If no response is seen after 10 mg total, the cause is likely non-opioid.
